badges.note: The ramp walked and cleared before the aircraft arrived, first time

badges.name: Envelope Kept
badges.note: Never inside the engine arc running, never a vehicle past the line, never a chock pulled early

challenges.name: Clean Ramp
challenges.note: No corrections anywhere in the turn

hazards.chock-pulled-early: You pulled the chocks with the bridge still on the aircraft. Nothing holds the aircraft then except its brakes, and a brake release with the bridge attached takes the door off.
hazards.cross-engine-arc: You walked through the engine's intake arc with the engine turning. A running narrow-body engine ingests a person from several metres in front of it, and the exhaust behind it will blow a baggage cart across the ramp.
hazards.under-fuselage-loading: You stood under the fuselage while the loader was moving against it. The loader's platform is a shear point against the aircraft skin, and there is no room to get out from under it.
hazards.vehicle-past-line: You drove ground equipment past the equipment-restraint line before the aircraft stopped and was chocked. Every year a piece of ground equipment strikes a moving aircraft on a ramp; the line exists to make that impossible.

interrupts.alert: A catering truck is coming up the stand and the equipment line cones are not where they should be.
interrupts.missNote: The truck came past the line with nothing marking it and stopped a metre off the fuselage. Ramp vehicle strikes on parked aircraft are the most common ground-damage claim there is, and the cone is the whole defence.
interrupts.why: The equipment restraint line is what stops a vehicle reaching the fuselage. It is reset for every turn because the last crew moved it, and a driver on a stand is steering to the cones, not to the paint.
interrupts.wrongNote: The vehicle is coming and the line is not set. Nothing else on this turn matters for the next ten seconds.

interrupts.alert: A tug has clipped the nose chock driving past. It is sitting a hand's width clear of the wheel.
interrupts.cue: The aircraft is not chocked. Re-set it before the bridge touches.
interrupts.missNote: You docked the bridge against an aircraft that was not chocked. If it had rolled, the bridge would have taken the door with it and everything in the jetway would have gone with the door.
interrupts.why: A chock that is not touching the tyre is not a chock. An aircraft on a sloping stand with the brakes released and the bridge docking against it has nothing holding it.
interrupts.wrongNote: The nose chock is the one that got kicked. Re-set it — the rest of the turn can wait.

lateNotes.allclear-signal: The all-clear is the last thing that happens, after the chocks and cones are back on the truck.
lateNotes.bridge-drive: The bridge comes to the door after the aircraft is stopped, chocked and coned.
lateNotes.gpu-connect: Ground power goes on after the aircraft is chocked and the engines are shut down.

name: Airport Ramp

passRule.note: stars >= 2 and no unsafe action (WebXR/shared/records.js passed())

steps.cue: Check the aircraft type, the stand, the equipment and who is on the headset.
steps.prompt: Check the aircraft type, the stand, the equipment and who is on the headset.
steps.title: Read the turn plan
steps.why: Stand geometry and the aircraft type on the turn plan decide where the chocks and cones actually go and how far the bridge has to travel to reach the door, none of which can be worked out once the aircraft is already on the stand. Under IATA's AHM 630 ground-operations guidance, the turn is planned on the ground before the aircraft is even on final approach.

steps.cue: Walk the area the aircraft will occupy and pick up every loose object you find.

itemNames.fod-strap: cargo strap on the lead-in line

itemNotes.fod-bolt: A bolt is lying on the stand where the engine will pass — one ingestion writes off an engine.
itemNotes.fod-strap: A cargo strap is across the lead-in line and will be blown into the intake or wrapped around a nose gear.

steps.prompt: Walk the area the aircraft will occupy and pick up every loose object you find.
steps.title: Walk the stand for FOD
steps.why: Foreign object damage is the single most expensive avoidable event on a ramp — one bolt through an intake writes off an engine, and a strap wrapped around a nose gear can bring an aircraft to a stop on the lead-in line. The walk happens before every single arrival regardless of how clean the stand looked last time, and what is found goes in the bin, never kicked aside for someone else to deal with.

steps.cue: Everything behind the equipment restraint line, brakes set, crew in hi-vis with hearing protection.
steps.prompt: Everything behind the equipment restraint line, brakes set, crew in hi-vis with hearing protection.
steps.title: Stage behind the line
steps.why: Until the aircraft is fully stopped and chocked, the equipment restraint line is the entire boundary between the ramp crew and a moving aeroplane the pilot cannot see past its own wingtips. Everyone and everything stays behind it, brakes set on the ground equipment and the crew in hi-vis with hearing protection on, per OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178 for the powered equipment already staged there.

steps.cue: Wands up, steady guidance down the lead-in line until the nosewheel reaches the stop bar.
steps.holdBreakNote: Signal rate out of band — the flight deck reads that as confusion. Steady the wands.
steps.prompt: Wands up, steady guidance down the lead-in line until the nosewheel reaches the stop bar.
steps.title: Marshal the aircraft in
steps.why: From the flight deck of a narrow-body, the pilot cannot see the nosewheel, the wingtips, or anything directly in front of the aircraft for the last stretch of the approach. The marshaller standing on the lead-in line, with steady wands and a steady walking rate, is the only reference the flight crew has for closing the final thirty metres onto the stand.

steps.cue: Give the stop when the nosewheel is on the stop bar — commit inside the band.

gauge.label: NOSEWHEEL
gauge.missNote: Off the stop bar — the bridge will not reach or the wingtip clearance is gone.

steps.prompt: Give the stop when the nosewheel is on the stop bar — commit inside the band.
steps.title: Stop on the mark
steps.why: The stop bar marking is calibrated for exactly one aircraft type on that stand: it is the one point where the jet bridge actually reaches the door and the wingtip still clears the adjacent stand's equipment. Stop a metre long or a metre short of that mark and one of those two things is no longer true, and neither is something the crew can fix after the aircraft is parked.

steps.cue: Nose chocks first, then the mains, then the cones at the wingtips and engines — and only then does anything else approach.
steps.outOfOrderNote: Nose, then mains, then cones — the aircraft is held before it is marked.
steps.prompt: Nose chocks first, then the mains, then the cones at the wingtips and engines — and only then does anything else approach.
steps.title: Chock and cone
steps.why: Chocks before any contact is the rule the whole ramp runs on, because until they are set nothing except the flight crew's own brakes is holding a parked aircraft on a stand that is rarely perfectly level. The cones at the wingtips and the engine mark the exact parts of the aircraft that a reversing tug or a swinging loader must never find with a mirror.

steps.cue: Connect ground power and plug the headset into the nose interphone.
steps.prompt: Connect ground power and plug the headset into the nose interphone.
steps.title: Ground power and headset
steps.why: Ground power connected first is what lets the engines and the auxiliary power unit actually shut down without losing electrics on the flight deck. The headset plugged into the nose interphone is the only direct line to the flight deck for the rest of the turn, and it is the same connection pushback will eventually happen on, so it is tested now rather than assumed.

steps.cue: Bring the bridge in steadily, watching the cab height and the door sill.
steps.holdBreakNote: Approach speed out of band — back off and bring it in steadily.
steps.prompt: Bring the bridge in steadily, watching the cab height and the door sill.
steps.title: Drive the bridge to the door
steps.why: A jet bridge driven fast into an aircraft door is a hull strike, and a hull strike on a narrow-body does not just delay this turn — it grounds the aircraft for inspection and cancels the next several flights on its rotation. Bringing it in steadily, watching the cab height against the door sill with the auto-level following, is what keeps the canopy from ever making first contact at speed.

steps.cue: Set the canopy against the fuselage and commit when the alignment is inside the band.

gauge.label: DOOR ALIGN
gauge.missNote: Canopy off centre — re-align before the door opens.

steps.prompt: Set the canopy against the fuselage and commit when the alignment is inside the band.
steps.title: Align and dock the bridge
steps.why: The bridge's canopy has to seal against the fuselage skin around the door, and the auto-level system keeps the cabin sill matched to the bridge floor as the aircraft physically rises on its gear while cargo and passengers come off. Docked off-centre, the seal leaks weather into the jetway and the sill develops a step that becomes a trip hazard for every passenger who crosses it.

steps.cue: Drive the belt loader to the cargo door at walking pace and stop short before raising the belt.

drag.missNote: Not stopped short of the fuselage — bring the loader in to the hold and stop before the platform touches the skin.

steps.prompt: Drive the belt loader to the cargo door at walking pace and stop short before raising the belt.
steps.title: Bring the belt loader to the hold
steps.why: Every vehicle that approaches a parked aircraft on the ramp does it at walking pace and stops short of the skin, under the same AHM 630 ground-support discipline that governs everything else on this turn. The last metre to the fuselage is closed with the loader's own platform, never by rolling the vehicle itself the rest of the way in.

steps.cue: Cones up, then chocks, then the all-clear on the headset with the chocks held up in view.
steps.outOfOrderNote: Cones, then chocks, then the all-clear — the aircraft is released last, and only once.
steps.prompt: Cones up, then chocks, then the all-clear on the headset with the chocks held up in view.
steps.title: Clear the stand and give the all-clear
steps.why: The cones come up first, the chocks second to last, and the all-clear last of all, given with the chocks held up in plain view of the flight deck. That specific sequence and that visible signal are the pilot's only proof, from inside a cockpit that cannot see the nosewheel, that nothing ground crew placed is still attached to or under their aircraft before they move it.

tagline: Gate turn: FOD walk and equipment restraint line, marshal onto the lead-in, chocks before anything touches it, cones set, ground power and headset to the flight deck, bridge to the door, loader at walking pace, all-clear only when chocks and cones are back
